extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy; scholars of Locke; those studying social-contract theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts normative criteria and definitions for family, marriage, servitude, the state of nature, and the constitution and origin of political (civil) society as presented in a political-philosophy treatise (Locke). Useful for analyzing when and how legitimate government and laws arise from consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ends of marriage / conjugal society
rubrics_metrics.description: The ends of matrimony/conjugal society are procreation and mutual support and assistance whilst together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke: 'For all the ends of marriage being to be obtained under politic government, as well as in the state of nature, the civil magistrate doth not abridge the right or power of either naturally necessary to those ends, viz. procreation and mutual support and assistance whilst they are together.' Emphasis that civil law should not remove rights necessary to these ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason for lasting conjugal bonds
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjugal bonds are made more lasting in mankind because the female is capable of conceiving again while previous offspring still depend on parental support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains a biological/social rationale for longer marital unions: fathers are obliged to continue conjugal society to provide for multiple dependent offspring; thus permanence of marriage is encouraged to secure provision for issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limits of husband's authority in marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: Husband's rule naturally falls to the man for matters of common interest and property, but this power reaches only the common concern and does not give the husband absolute authority over the wife's life or peculiar rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke stresses limits: 'the wife in the full and free possession of what by contract is her peculiar right, and gives the husband no more power over her life than she has over his.' The wife may separate where natural right or contract allows; conjugal power is not monarchical or absolute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugal society may be determinable by consent/condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriage, being a voluntary compact, can be made determinable (terminable) by consent, at a certain time, or upon certain conditions, unless positive law makes it perpetual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke raises possibility that where no positive law requires permanence, parties could contract for limited or conditional conjugal bonds—i.e., marital duration is subject to agreement in the state of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between family (domestic) and political society
rubrics_metrics.description: A family (master, wife, children, servants, slaves) though resembling a little commonwealth in order, differs fundamentally in constitution, power and end from a political society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Family rule is limited in time and extent over individuals; the paterfamilias lacks legislative power of life and death over members (except slave) and cannot exercise absolute authority as a commonwealth's sovereign can. Use this to distinguish private/domestic authority from public/political authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master-servant versus slavery distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: A servant is someone who sells his services for wages (temporary power defined by contract); a slave is a captive taken in just war and thereby subjected to absolute dominion and arbitrary power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke: servants' subjection is contractual and limited, while slaves, having 'forfeited their lives, and with it their liberties, and lost their estates', cannot be considered part of civil society and are incapable of property in that state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/criterion for political (civil) society
rubrics_metrics.description: Political society exists where every member has quitted his natural power to judge and punish breaches of the law of nature and has resigned that power into the hands of the community (or its magistrates), creating common established law and judicature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key lines: 'there, and there only is political society, where every one of the members hath quitted this natural power, resigned it up into the hands of the community ...' and 'Those who are united into one body, and have a common established law and judicature to appeal to, with authority to decide controversies between them, and punish offenders, are in civil society one with another.' Use resignation of private judgment and presence of public law/judges as the test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right and purpose of legislative/executive power
rubrics_metrics.description: The commonwealth (legislative) has the power to set down punishments for transgressions and to employ the force of its members for execution of judgments, all for preservation of property and public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke explains origins: by consenting, individuals authorize the society to make laws as public good requires, and to use members' assistance in executing those laws. Emphasizes law-making and sanctioning as central functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent as sole source of legitimate political subjection
rubrics_metrics.description: No one can be put out of natural freedom and subjected to political power without his own consent; the only way to divest natural liberty is by agreeing with others to unite into a community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke: 'The only way whereby any one divests himself of his natural liberty, and puts on the bonds of civil society, is by agreeing with other men to join and unite into a community.' Use voluntary agreement as criterion of legitimate government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority rule as basis for collective action
rubrics_metrics.description: Once individuals consent to make a community, that community acts as one body by the will and determination of the majority; the act of the majority is taken as the act of the whole unless otherwise agreed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke offers practical reasoning: unanimity is next to impossible; to be one body the greater force must carry it. The majority's decisions bind every individual who consented to the social compact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community gives up only powers necessary to ends of union
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who unite into a society give up all the power necessary to the ends for which they unite (preservation of property, peace, security) to the majority of the community, unless they expressly agree otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke: 'Whosoever therefore out of a state of nature unite into a community, must be understood to give up all the power, necessary to the ends for which they unite into society, to the majority of the community.' Use 'necessary to the ends' as limiting principle on transferred authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute monarchy incompatible with civil society
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute monarchy, where the prince has all legislative and executive power and there is no impartial judge or appeal, is inconsistent with civil society because subjects have no appeal on earth and are effectively in the state of nature with respect to the prince.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues: 'Where-ever therefore any persons are ... who have not such an authority to appeal to, for the decision of any difference between them, there those persons are still in the state of nature.' Absolute princes leave subjects without redress and thus cannot constitute a civil society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for standing laws and judges to prevent private judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil society requires standing rules and laws, known beforehand, and judges with authority to decide controversies and redress injuries; this prevents every man acting as judge in his own case and endless strife.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke emphasizes transition from private execution to public law: 'they come to be umpire, by settled standing rules, indifferent, and the same to all parties.' Laws should make duties and penalties known; absence of such laws invites tyranny or anarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/functional origins of government forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Although governments often appear monarchical in origin (e.g., paternal rule transitioning to rule by one), this is compatible with the view that governments properly begin by consent, and early monarchy often arose as a practical choice for defense and leadership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke notes familial/paternal beginnings and practical reasons (war leadership, simplicity) for early monarchical forms, but emphasizes that ultimate legitimacy derives from consent: 'they used their natural freedom, to set up him, whom they judged the ablest.'
